title: Navigation for a creative studio
excerpt: Label the site with jobs the buyer already names, and keep one path that starts a project. Department names make them translate before they can move.
alt: Two white smartwatch mockups on a plain light background, one showing the face and one the back, as distinct as two paths in a navigation bar.
caption: Two white smartwatches, one face and one back, on a plain background. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What labels belong in the navigation?
faqs.answer: The jobs a visitor has: see the work, understand what you sell, learn who decides, and start a project. Work, Services, About, and Start a project cover most studios. Department names such as Lab or Offerings make the buyer translate.

faqs.question: How many items is too many?
faqs.answer: More than five usually means something in the bar is for you, not for them. Careers you are not hiring for, a client login, and legal pages belong in the footer. A mega-menu of every project hides the map.

faqs.question: Should the phone menu differ from the desktop bar?
faqs.answer: No. Same jobs, same order, same words for the action. The phone menu is where many buyers will first move. A second taxonomy is a second site you will forget to update.

markdown:
Creative studio website navigation is a map of jobs, not a list of departments. For a client who has already seen fifty portfolios, the labels should match words they already use, and one path should start a project.

If the bar says Studio, Offerings, Insights, and Contact, the buyer has to translate before they can move. Translation is a tax. On a site whose only job is to prove judgment, a tax in the first second is a mistake.

## Jobs, not departments

List the jobs a visitor actually has. See the work. Understand what you sell. Learn who decides. Start a project. Those four jobs cover almost every serious visit. A fifth, such as a journal, belongs in the bar only if a new client would use it to judge you. A journal that exists to keep a content calendar full does not belong beside Work.

[The W3C's overview of WCAG](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) describes a usable site as perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. Navigation is the operable and understandable part people touch first. Links need a purpose a person can name. The same words should mean the same destination every time. A label that changes personality between the header and the footer fails that, even when the type is beautiful.

Department names fail because they describe you. Creative. Strategy. Production. Lab. The buyer does not have a job called "lab." They have a job called "see if these people can choose." Name that job in their verb. Work. Services. About. Start a project.

Do not add a label because a competitor has it. Insights, Journal, Stories, and News blur together. If you publish proof, call it Work or Projects. If you publish writing that helps a buyer decide, call it by the decision it supports, or put the best of it inside the relevant service. A lonely blog link in the bar is not a strategy. It is a spare room.

## Labels they already use

Say the words out loud as if you were the client on a phone, telling a colleague where to click. "Go to work." "Look at services." "Start a project." If the sentence sounds odd, the label is odd. "Engage with our universe" cannot be said to a colleague without irony. Irony is not a navigation system.

Keep labels short. One or two words. The bar is not the place for a slogan. The homepage headline can hold the decision. The nav holds the map. When a label needs a paragraph, it is not a label. It is a page that has not been named yet.

Match the labels to the pages you wrote. If the services page is titled in the buyer's language, the nav item should be the same language. If the proof pages are case studies, do not call the index "Selected atmospheres." Consistency here is not a brand quirk. It is how a skeptical buyer learns the site in one pass.

Proper names of famous projects can sit inside the work index. They should not all sit in the global bar. A bar with eight project names is a portfolio dumped into chrome. The buyer wanted a map. Give them a map, then a well-labeled index.

## One path that starts a project

One item in the bar is the action. Start a project. It should look like the action, not like another essay. A text link is enough if it is the same phrase the rest of the site uses. A button is fine if you have not already used three other button styles. The point is singularity. A buyer should never wonder which of two "get in touch" items is the real one.

That path should land on a page that says what happens next, how fast you actually reply, and what to have ready. Do not point the primary nav item at a mailto with no context, and do not point it at a ten-field form. The nav promises a start. The page has to keep the promise. If the page is not ready, the nav item is a lie.

Do not repeat the action as Work With Us, Contact, Let's Talk, and Book a Call across the same bar. Pick the phrase. Use it in the header, after the proof, and on the pricing page. Repetition of one phrase builds confidence. Repetition of four synonyms builds a maze.

On small sites the action can be the last item, easy to find and easy to ignore until they are ready. Do not pin a chat bubble over it. A bubble that opens an unnamed inbox competes with the path you just designed. If you want a conversation, send them to the page that explains the conversation.

## How many items

Four or five items is the useful range for this kind of studio. Work, Services, About, and Start a project. Add Pricing if the pricing page is honest enough to stand in the bar. If pricing is a tease, leave it off the bar and link it from Services, or fix the page. Do not hide a real pricing page out of shyness, and do not promote an empty one out of habit.

Drop anything that is for you rather than for them. A login for clients can live in the footer or on a known URL. The client portal, where brand files and project updates live after delivery, is a tool for people already in the work. It does not need equal billing with Work on the public bar. Careers, if you are not hiring, should not occupy a slot. A legal page belongs in the footer.

Mega-menus are rarely the answer for a studio of this size. A panel that opens onto every project, every service, and a featured essay hides the map under a second homepage. Use a simple list. If Work needs a submenu, two groups are enough: the kinds of jobs, not every case study. The index page can do the rest.

Test the bar by removing the logo and the pictures. Can you still tell what the site is for? If the labels only make sense next to a reel, the labels are dependent on mood. Rewrite them until they work in a text email.

## The same map on a phone

Most of these buyers will judge the site on a phone, often from a link a colleague sent. The nav has to survive that. A menu icon is fine. A menu that opens into a different set of names is not. The phone menu and the desktop bar should list the same jobs in the same order.

Put Start a project where a thumb can reach it, inside the menu and again on the first screen of the homepage. Do not bury it under a newsletter field, a social row, and a paragraph about the studio's philosophy. Those can exist. They are not the map.

Keep the open menu readable. Large type. Real labels. Enough contrast that the words are still words on a bright sidewalk. WCAG's point about perceivable text is not a special project you do later. It is the reason the menu works outside your office. Do not set nav type in a hairline weight because it looked elegant on a calibrated monitor.

Do not auto-advance anything behind the open menu. A reel that keeps playing under a nav panel makes the labels harder to trust. Pause the motion. Let them read. The decision you are selling is already hard to see. Do not cover it with chrome that moves.

## What the labels should refuse

Refuse synonyms that you added for search. One page should not be linked as Work, Projects, Case Studies, and Portfolio from four different places with four destinations. Pick the destination and the word. Elsewhere, link that word.

Refuse a label you cannot staff. If there is no About page with names and standards, do not put About in the bar as a promise. If Services is still a grid of moods, fix the page before you give it a permanent slot. Navigation makes a contract. Breaking it on the next click is how a careful buyer decides you will break it in the project too.

Refuse cleverness that needs a tooltip. A symbol with no text, a hamburger that is actually a face, a menu named with a single letter from the logo. You are not short of opportunities to show craft. The bar is the opportunity to be understood.

When the map is stable, the pictures have to obey it. A nav label called Work is a promise that the images under it show decisions, not an unexplained reel. [Photography direction for a creative studio](/blog/photography-direction-for-a-creative-studio) is the next piece to write, because the frames are part of the argument the labels just made. Get the words true first. Then aim the camera at the decision.

If you want help putting the map and the pages into one site, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the labels you have now, including the ones you are slightly ashamed of. The call should leave you with a shorter list and one path that starts a project, not with a new slogan for the bar.
